bio.en: Naomi Ionita is a Partner at Menlo Ventures, was one of the first B2B product-led growth leaders at Evernote and Invoice2go, and an early mentor at Reforge.
bio.zh: 娜奥米·约尼塔（Naomi Ionita）是 Menlo Ventures 的合伙人，曾是 Evernote 与 Invoice2go 最早的一批 B2B 产品驱动增长（PLG）领导者，也是 Reforge 的早期导师。

summary.en: Naomi delivers a master class on monetization and pricing, covering common founder mistakes and concrete experiments to set price. She introduces the "Modern Growth Stack" of tools that automate growth work and discusses where AI fits. The episode also warns that early growth is sometimes achieved at the expense of revenue.
summary.zh: 娜奥米带来了一堂关于变现与定价的课，涵盖创始人常犯的错误，以及设定价格的具体实验方法。她提出了能自动化增长工作的"现代增长栈"（Modern Growth Stack）工具概念，并讨论 AI 的位置。本期还提醒：早期增长有时会以牺牲收入为代价。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Do not set it and forget it. I see companies do this, where they labor over designs and features. And they build this perfect product that's delightful to use. And then pricing's sort of plucked out of thin air, and then they don't revisit it. This was Evernote. It was many, many years before we went back and overhauled the pricing. So, think about your pricing just like you do your roadmap. Every 6 to 12 months, there's probably something meaningful that you're launching for users. So, treat that as an opportunity to revisit your monetization strategy and making sure you're compensated appropriately.
turns.zh: 切不可一劳永逸地设定好价格就不管不问了。我见过很多公司这样做，他们在设计和功能上下了很大功夫，打造出一个使用体验极佳的完美产品。但定价却完全凭空设定，之后就再也不调整了。Evernote就曾犯过这样的错误。直到多年后，我们才重新审视并彻底调整了定价策略。所以，您要像规划产品路线图一样审视定价策略。每隔6到12个月，您很可能就会为用户推出一些有意义的新功能。借此机会，您可以重新评估盈利策略，确保获得合理的回报。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Perfect. So, I'm a partner at Menlo Ventures. I focus on early-stage SaaS from seed to series B. I started my career in engineering and consulting before getting into tech back in '06. Fell in love with product. Did some new product development at a big media company before business school. And while at business school, I spent time at the Design Institute at Stanford. So, this was an opportunity to kind of bridge my analytical background with this refreshing view on human-centered design and learning from the founder of IDEO. (04:56): So, brought that with me then to Evernote back in 2011, early days over there. I was there from about 10 to 100 million users. And over that arc, I shifted from more of a core product role to starting our growth product function. This was super organic. I started just collaborating with colleagues from across the business, come up with hypotheses, do user research, run experiments, drive metrics. This was a new way of building product back then. This was a decade ago, so the acronym PLG had not been coined yet. And I really just thought of myself as a user and data-driven product person. (05:33): After Evernote, I joined a bootstrapped mobile SMB company called Invoice2go. It was the top-grossing business app at the time. There, I built teams across product, data, growth engineering, design and research, and again, focused on product-led growth and monetization. Over those two jobs, I found myself doing a lot more advising and speaking on the side on these topics. And my board members used to farm me out to their companies to help their founders think through things around product growth and pricing and various topics like that. And Reforge came together at the same time, so I would come in and speak on topics through that community. So, that really accelerated my transition into venture. I realized how much I love having that portfolio view of the world and helping founders look around corners. So, I think it's an incredible privilege to get to do the work that I do.
turns.zh: 好的。我是Menlo Ventures的合伙人。我的专注领域是早期阶段的SaaS，从种子轮到B轮融资。我在2006年进入科技行业之前，曾在工程和咨询领域工作过。后来爱上了产品设计。在攻读商学院之前，我在斯坦福设计学院深造。这段经历让我得以将分析背景与以人为中心的设计理念相结合，并向IDEO的创始人学习。（04:56）2011年，我加入Evernote，见证了其从1000万到1亿用户的飞跃。在此期间，我从核心产品角色转向建立增长产品团队。这完全是自然而然的过程。我开始与不同部门的同事合作，提出假设、进行用户研究、开展实验并追踪数据。这在当时是一种全新的产品开发方式。十年前，“PLG”这个术语还未被创造出来。我当时只把自己视为以用户和数据为导向的产品经理。（05:33）离开Evernote后，我加入了一家自筹资金的移动SMB公司Invoice2go。当时它是应用商店收入最高的商业应用。在那里，我组建了涵盖产品、数据、增长工程、设计和研究的团队，再次专注于产品主导的增长和变现。在这两份工作中，我发现自己越来越多地为这些主题提供咨询和演讲。我的董事会成员经常把我派到他们的公司，帮助创始人思考产品增长、定价等各种问题。与此同时，Reforge也应运而生，我开始在该社区分享这些话题。这真正加速了我向风投领域的转型。我意识到自己非常喜欢这种审视全局的视角，帮助创始人预见未来机遇。因此，能从事现在的工作，我深感荣幸。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One thing you mentioned is Evernote. I don't know how much you can talk about this, but they just got sold, right? Someone bought Evernote. And if I think back to Evernote, it feels like they could have been Notion, which is killing it right now. Any thoughts on what maybe they missed and didn't turn into Notion along the way?
turns.zh: 你提到的Evernote。我不知道你能透露多少信息，但他们刚被收购了，对吧？有人买下了Evernote。回想起来，Evernote本可以成为Notion那样火爆的应用。关于他们可能错过的机会，你有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah. We're going to clear some cobwebs here. It's been a while. But one challenge that Evernote really struggled with was this evolution from single-player to multiplayer to team to enterprise. It's a chasm that a lot of bottom-up SaaS businesses struggle to cross. Evernote was philosophically antisocial. It was meant to be your second brain, kind of your personal tool. And I think that capped the company's growth potential. I always used to say you can't retrofit collaboration. You have to be collaboration-first. And a lot of companies now really take that for granted. But back in mid-2000s, this was kind of a new way of building product. And so we missed that bridge. (07:20): If companies do that well, it benefits every metric. That bridge from single-player to multiplayer. Acquisition goes up. You grow organically through referrals and shared workflows. Retention goes up because now you have these shared workflows that are incredibly sticky. Employees are accountable to each other to say, "This is how work gets done." Design in Figma, roadmap planning and ticketing in Jira are linear. It just becomes the default platform. And modernization goes up. Revenue scales with usage. And so the more people using it, the more they use it. You start tripping the wire on paying more and more over time. And so Evernote really struggled in crossing that chasm from the prosumer tool of choice that employees wall-to-wall were using, but never became this larger high-ACV contract from a sales perspective.
turns.zh:
是啊。我们现在要清理一些积压的工作。已经有一段时间了。但Evernote真正面临的挑战是从单人用户到多人用户，再到团队用户，再到企业用户的演变。这是许多自下而上的SaaS企业难以跨越的鸿沟。Evernote在理念上是反社交的。它本应成为你的第二大脑，是你的个人工具。我认为这限制了公司的增长潜力。我过去常说，无法事后补救协作问题。必须以协作为先。如今很多公司都把这视为理所当然。但在2000年代中期，这是一种全新的产品开发方式。因此我们错过了那个桥梁。

（07:20）：如果企业能做好这点，各方面都会受益。从单人用户到多人用户的桥梁。获取用户量增加。通过推荐和共享工作流程实现自然增长。留存率提升，因为现在有了这些极具粘性的共享工作流程。员工会互相监督：“工作就是这样完成的。”Figma中的设计、Jira中的路线图规划和工单管理都是线性的。它最终会成为默认平台。现代化程度提升。收入随使用量增长。使用人数越多，收入越高。最终用户会自然而然地愿意支付更多费用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's always easy in hindsight to see what could have been better, what could have worked out, what didn't work out. So, what are you going to do? You mentioned monetization. And I know that you spent a lot of time with founders working on pricing, monetization, especially using monetization as a lever for growth. And so I want to spend some time there to pick your brain about what founders and growth teams can do and how they should think about monetization in terms of growth.
turns.zh: 是啊，后见之明总是能看清本可以做得更好的地方、本可以成功的地方，以及未能成功的地方。那么接下来你打算怎么做？你提到了货币化。我知道你花了很多时间与创始人一起研究定价、货币化，特别是将货币化作为增长的杠杆。因此我想花些时间向你请教，创始人和增长团队可以做些什么，以及他们应该如何从增长的角度思考货币化问题。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you also have this cool concept that you've been developing that you call the Modern Growth Stack, which is kind of this play on modern data stack. And so I want to spend some time there.
turns.zh: 然后你还开发了一个很酷的概念，叫做“现代增长栈”，这是对现代数据栈的一种玩味。因此我想花些时间探讨一下这个概念。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So, to dive into that first topic of monetization, if you think about when you're starting a company, what are some of the biggest challenges you face? Start building a product, especially a B2B product, I always think about pricing and trying to figure out how much to charge, how to charge, your pricing model, how to evolve your pricing, when to charge, all these things. And so I know that you work with founders helping them figure these sorts of things out. And so maybe a first question here is just what do you find startups most often miss or get wrong when they're starting to think about monetization?
turns.zh: 不错。那么首先来谈谈货币化这个话题。如果你考虑创办一家公司，面临的最大挑战是什么？特别是B2B产品，我总是会想到定价，如何定价，定价模式，如何调整定价，何时收费，所有这些问题。因此我知道你会帮助创始人解决这些问题。那么第一个问题是，初创公司在开始思考货币化时，最常忽视或做错的是什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: There's a lot to cover here. I'll cover a few missteps that I think are most common. One is waiting too long to monetize. Another one is underpricing. And this isn't just setting the base price too low, but it's also leaving money on the table by not offering different plans to cater to different segments. And the third one is all too often with pricing, people set it and forget it. So, this idea that when your product development work is never done, neither is your pricing, and you need to combat that along the way. So, those are three areas I think we can cover here. (09:47): Maybe starting with one, I can jump right in, I think waiting too long to monetize. The beginning of a startup's journey is all about creating something of value. Right? That's the whole point. Hopefully, founders have some unique market insight or some authenticity around a pain point and some novel solution that's going to change the world. So, that business value is really critical. But the other side of the same coin is being properly compensated for that value as a business. I understand the vulnerability of being a new startup. You just want people to use your product. And I view that early free beta user feedback loop as an R&D cost to make sure you're building the best possible product and that they're driving a lot of value. (10:28): But I see companies way too long to make that shift from building a product to building a business. And I think that's the true signal of product-market fit, is ultimately having people open up their wallets and pay you, so looking for people to get to that end goal. And so again, these things aren't mutually exclusive. You're going to create business value, but you're going to be compensated for it and prioritize your roadmap over time so that you're building based on what people actually want and are willing to pay you for. (10:55): So, when you don't monetize, I think you're doing yourself a disservice. The things that I see as the pain of leaving money on the table, you're inadvertently cheapening your product. People attribute a lower dollar value or a $0 value to what you've built. You're missing out on critical feedback loops to understand what people are willing to pay. And you're shooting your future self in the foot because this is the other problem, is at some point you're going to start charging, and you're going to experience some backlash. So, it's nice to get ahead of that. A few things to think about, kind of food for thought around delaying and kicking the can down the road from a monetization-
turns.zh: 接下来要讲的内容很多。我会重点分析我认为最常见的三个错误做法。第一个是等待太久才开始变现。第二个是定价过低。这里不只是指基础价格定得过低，还包括不提供差异化套餐以满足不同客户需求，从而白白错失商机。第三个问题是人们在定价方面往往一劳永逸。我认为产品开发永无止境，定价工作也应持续优化，因此我们需要不断克服这些挑战。以下是我们可以探讨的三个方面。（09:47）：或许先从第一个入手，我会直接切入——等待太久才开始变现。创业之旅的初期阶段，关键在于创造有价值的产品，对吧？这才是核心所在。希望创始人能拥有独特的市场洞察力，或针对某个痛点提出真实的解决方案，从而改变世界。这种商业价值至关重要。但另一方面，作为企业，你需要为这种价值获得合理回报。我理解初创公司容易陷入困境——你只想让用户使用你的产品。我把早期免费测试用户反馈循环视为研发成本，确保产品质量上乘，同时为用户创造巨大价值。（10:28）：但我发现许多公司在从产品开发到商业化转型上拖延太久。产品与市场匹配的真正标志，是用户愿意为你的产品买单。因此要关注最终目标。这些方面并非相互排斥。你需要创造商业价值，同时通过路线图优化，确保产品符合用户需求并获得支付意愿。（10:55）：不变现等于自毁前程。错失价值回报等于贬低产品价值。人们会对你的成果给予低估或零价值评判。你将错失关键反馈，无法了解用户支付意愿。更糟糕的是，当你最终开始收费时，可能会遭遇用户抵触。因此提前做好准备至关重要。关于延迟变现和拖延问题，这里有几点值得思考——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, just to reinforce that, your general piece of advice is if you're building a B2B product, start charging immediately. Don't give it away for free. At least have some... You could probably give it away for free but make it clear, "We're going to charge you this much soon." How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 再强调一下，对于B2B产品，你的核心建议是立即收费，别免费赠送。至少要明确说明：“我们很快就会开始收费。”对此你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, I don't think those are mutually exclusive. So, this isn't to say that I don't like freemium models. Evernote was the darling of freemium over a decade ago. So, I'm still a big believer in that. It's more a question of where you put the paywall. How much do you give up for free? And then how do you price and package a paid version of your product? So, freemium is all about getting that top-of-funnel excitement, getting people to build habit formation. You're collapsing time to value. You're building habit formation. You're building all these champions to use your product. But the idea is to shepherd them along into a paid version of your product and to, again, not delay the idea of, "What should our premium features even be? What should that paid plan even look like?" Again, going back to the misstep at Evernote, I think there was always a premium plan, but it didn't really bridge into enterprise. So, we can talk more about that.
turns.zh: 是的，我不认为这两者是相互排斥的。所以，我并不是说我不喜欢免费增值模式。十多年前，Evernote就是免费增值模式的典范。所以，我仍然非常看好这种模式。关键在于如何设置付费门槛。免费版能提供多少功能？然后如何定价和打包付费版本？免费增值模式的核心在于激发用户兴趣，帮助他们养成使用习惯。它能缩短用户从感知到价值的时间，培养用户习惯，培养种子用户。但关键是引导他们升级到付费版本，并且尽早思考：我们的付费功能应该是什么样的？付费套餐该如何设计？再回头看Evernote的失误，虽然一直有付费套餐，但它没有真正切入企业级市场。关于这点，我们可以深入探讨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is kind of a tangent, I know, because you have these two other pieces of underpricing and setting it and forgetting it. Been talked about, but do you have any advice for deciding what goes into freemium and what-
turns.zh: 我知道这有点跑题了，因为你们之前讨论了定价过低和设置后就遗忘的问题。这些都被提及过，但对于决定哪些功能纳入免费增值模式，哪些功能不纳入——

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: If it gets you to the aha moment, that path to habit formation, that has to be free. That's the core utility of your product. And so the idea is that in that first session or first day, someone's getting to see the delight and saying, "Oh, my God. I'm never going back to the old way. This is how X gets done." If you're looking for some virality or network effect, that's the other thing. Your free users, you might not be getting revenue from, but the idea is that they help you manage CAC. So, these are folks that are driving organic growth for you and helping reduce the incremental cost of your next set of users. So, that's another part of the math equation to think about in giving up revenue.
turns.zh: 如果能让用户产生“啊哈”时刻，进入习惯养成阶段，那这些功能就必须免费。这是产品核心的实用价值。因此，核心思路是在用户首次使用或第一天体验中，让他们感受到愉悦感，并感叹：“天哪，我再也回不到旧方式了。用X来完成这件事真是太棒了。” 如果你想追求病毒式传播或网络效应，那是另一回事。免费用户虽然不能直接带来收入，但他们能帮助降低客户获取成本。因此，这些用户能为你带来自然增长，帮助降低新用户的增量成本。这也是在放弃收入时需要考虑的数学方程式的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also have this model that you didn't mention that you mentioned in a previous chat we were having offline of this idea of day one versus day 100, stuff people need on day one versus what they need down the road. Do you still believe in that? And what should people know about that?
turns.zh: 你提到的另一个模式，我们之前线下聊过，就是“第一天”和“第100天”的对比，用户第一天需要什么，未来需要什么。你现在还相信这个观点吗？人们对此应该了解什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I do believe in that. That was tied to... We had done this experiment at my last company, Invoice2go, where... Typically on the demand curve, the higher you raise the price, the average revenue per user or ARPU, the lower the conversion rate. So, these things are inversely correlated. And we were able to do this rebalancing of our pricing and packaging so that we actually doubled our upgrade rate from our starter plan to our pro plan.
turns.zh: 我确实相信这个观点。我们在上一家公司Invoice2go做过实验……通常在需求曲线上，价格越高，用户平均收入（ARPU）越高，转化率越低。所以这些是负相关的。我们通过重新平衡定价和打包策略，成功将初级计划用户升级到专业计划的比例翻了一番。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: ... We doubled our upgrade rate from our starter plan to our pro plan while also increasing the price of the pro plan. So, to actually get twice as many people to upgrade while paying something like 30% more for that new plan is pretty rare to get the compounding benefits of that. And what we did was thought a lot about what is a day one premium feature? What is a premium feature that you can get value from the very first time you engage with the product? That's different than your day 100 features. Those are the ones that represent more advanced functionality. Maybe they're ones where the value is derived from having a certain scale of data in the platform. (14:37): And so, those you shouldn't waste cognitive load for your users to have to even understand or try to appreciate when they're first getting going. Push those into a more advanced pro version of your product, and monetize them down the road through an upsell. So, big believer in how do you really keep pricing simple? And we've all seen those SaaS pricing pages where there's a laundry list or just a gnarly matrix of features and functionality. So, do what you can to think about that journey for a user and how they're going to continue to increase value with your product over time, and how you can map your pricing and packaging against that journey.
turns.zh: ……我们将初级计划升级到专业计划的比率提高了一倍，同时也提高了专业计划的价格。因此，要让两倍数量的用户升级到专业计划，同时让他们为新计划多支付约30%的费用，获得这种复合效益是相当难得的。我们为此深入思考了：什么是产品上线第一天的付费功能？什么是用户首次使用产品就能获得价值的付费功能？这与100天后的功能是不同的。后者代表着更高级的功能，可能需要在平台中积累一定规模的数据才能体现其价值。（14:37）因此，对于用户而言，这些功能无需耗费太多精力去理解或评估。可以将它们整合到更高级的专业版产品中，并在未来通过追加销售实现变现。所以，我非常认同如何真正保持定价的简洁性。我们都见过那些SaaS定价页面，上面罗列着长长的功能清单或复杂的功能矩阵。因此，要尽可能从用户的使用路径出发，思考他们如何随着时间推移不断提升对产品的价值，以及如何根据这一路径调整定价和套餐设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that framework, because it's so straightforward and simple. As you use it, you'll need more enterprise features innately, because you're sharing it more widely. Your head of security's going to be like, "What are you doing with this thing?" Your finance team's going to be like, "Oh, how do we pay for this thing?" And so, that's a really nice simple way of thinking about what to put in freemium in your free plan versus not. So, glad we touched on that. Okay, so we were going through the three things that companies and founders do wrong when they're starting to price. And so, the first you said was they go too late and I tangentized us, so I'll give it back to you to keep going through this.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个框架，因为它非常直接和简单。当你实际应用它时，你会自然地需要更多企业级功能，因为你的产品被更广泛地使用了。你的安全主管会问：“你用这个东西做什么？” 你的财务团队会问：“哦，我们怎么为这个东西付费？” 因此，这是一种非常好的简单思维方式，用于决定在免费计划中加入哪些免费增值功能。这部分内容讲得很好，很高兴我们提到了这一点。好的，我们已经讨论了公司和创始人在定价初期常犯的三个错误。首先你提到他们定价太晚，我稍微跑题了，现在把话题交给你，继续讲下去。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: [inaudible 00:15:53] This is by far the most common issue. And so, one framework I like to use here is matching price to value. When you do that, you create alignment with your user. So, this entails picking the right value metric. So, this is the unit of value that they derive from using your product, and it creates this natural escalator, because as people use it more, you get paid more over time. SaaS was historically built on a seat based model. That's been historical SaaS pricing. And now with the rise of PLG, we've seen more of these usage based approaches gaining speed, so that's pretty exciting to see. Whether it's number of API calls or messages sent or terabytes of storage used or words written, this usage-based approach really matches price to value over the lifetime of a customer. The other thing that happens when you match price to value is it helps you understand who you're building for, and it lets you target different customer segments. (16:46): In doing that, you're able to better serve each segment, but you're also able to maximize revenue for the business. Evernote always had a business model. From its beginning, it had $45 a year for an annual subscription. And this set the foundation for the company and tens of millions in revenue, early revenue growth, but the approach was suboptimal. So, as a growth team, we started doing surveys. I was really curious to understand why people converted from our free version to our premium subscription. And one of the most popular answers without fail was, "Well, I just feel guilty. I use it so much. I get so much value from it that I just feel obligated to pay." And take that in for a second, because if guilt is one of the main reasons why people are paying you, then your free version is too good, and you are leaving money on the table. (17:36): So, a single premium tier is often a mistake, and you're going to be leaving money on the table for specific segments, and it's important to drill down and understand who those are. Our additional research helped us understand that brand-new users with low perceived value of Evernote looked at it like their Apple Notepad app that was pre-installed on their device. And so, they couldn't understand the idea of paying $45 for Evernote. But then we talked to avid users, and these were people that were cross client using it on desktop and mobile, every device they had. They were using it for work and personal, they were leveraging OCR capabilities and the web clipper, and it was truly their second brain. They could not imagine life without it. And these people were floored that they were only paying $45 a year. They told us that they were getting hundreds of value from Evernote. (18:28): Here, the perceived value for avid users was far outpacing what we were asking from them. And this intuition and research really led to a bifurcated strategy of having different plans for different personas based on the value they got from the product and their willingness to pay.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，这是最常见的问题。因此，我在这里喜欢使用的一个框架是将价格与价值相匹配。当你这样做时，就能与用户达成共识。这就需要选择合适的价值衡量标准。所谓价值单位，是用户使用你的产品所获得的收益，这会形成一个自然的增益机制——因为用户使用得越多，你就能随时间赚取更多收益。传统的SaaS模式基于座位计费，但随着PLG（产品生命周期定价）兴起，基于使用量的定价方式正越来越普及，这确实令人振奋。无论是API调用次数、发送的消息数量、使用的存储空间还是输入的文字量，这种基于使用量的定价方式能在客户整个生命周期内将价格与价值紧密结合。将价格与价值匹配的另一个好处是，能让你更清楚服务的对象是谁，并有针对性地开发不同客户群体。（16:46）通过这种方式，你既能更好地服务每个细分市场，又能为企业实现收入最大化。Evernote一直有自己的商业模式。从一开始，它就推出了年费45美元的订阅服务，这为公司奠定了基础，早期实现了数千万美元的收入增长，但这种定价方式并不理想。因此，作为增长团队，我们开始开展调研。我特别想了解人们为何从免费版升级到付费版。其中最常见的回答是：“嗯，我只是觉得内疚。我用得太多了，从中获得了巨大价值，所以觉得有义务付费。” 这值得深思——如果内疚感是用户付费的主要原因，那么免费版就做得太好了，这无异于把钱留在桌上。（17:36）单一的付费层级往往是错误的，你会为特定客户群体留下收益空间。深入研究后我们发现，新用户对Evernote的感知价值很低，他们把它视为设备预装的苹果记事本应用，无法理解为何要为Evernote付费。但与活跃用户交流后发现，这些用户在桌面和移动设备上无缝切换客户端，工作和生活场景中都离不开它。他们会使用OCR功能和网页剪辑器，视其为第二大脑，离不开它。这些用户对每年仅需45美元的收费感到震惊，表示Evernote为他们创造了数百美元的价值。（18:28）活跃用户的感知价值远超你的收费标准。这种直觉和研究最终促成了基于用户价值和支付意愿的差异化定价策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. When I heard you say that it costs $45 for a year, that sounds way too low. So I could see how that sets the pattern for Evernote just not making enough money over the long term. Cool. And then the third was that you don't evolve your pricing, right? That's like the third biggest mistake.
turns.zh: 有道理。听你说一年45美元，感觉太低了。所以我能理解这为什么导致Evernote长期赚不到足够的钱。不错。然后第三个是你们不调整定价，对吧？这应该是第三大错误。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yes. So, do not set it and forget it. I see companies do this where they labor over designs and features, and they build this perfect product that's delightful to use, and then pricing plucked out of thin air, and then they don't revisit it. This was Evernote. It was many, many years before we went back and overhauled the pricing. So, think about your pricing just like you do your roadmap. Every six to 12 months, there's probably something meaningful that you're launching for users. Treat that as an opportunity to revisit your monetization strategy and making sure you're compensated appropriately.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，不要设定好价格后就置之不理。我见过很多公司这样做——他们费尽心思设计产品功能，打造出令人愉悦的使用体验，却随意定价，之后又不进行调整。Evernote就曾出现过这种情况。直到多年后我们才重新审视定价策略。所以，要像对待产品路线图一样对待定价策略。每六到十二个月，公司就会推出一项对用户有意义的新功能，把这当作重新审视盈利策略、确保获得合理回报的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What advice do you have for founders around just how to decide in your initial price? Clearly Evernote didn't get that correct, and I'm sure you've learned a lot from that and then other companies you've worked with. How do you actually decide what to start charging?
turns.zh: 对于初创企业如何确定初始定价，你有什么建议？显然Evernote在这方面做得不够，我相信你从中吸取了教训，也从合作过的其他公司获得了经验。那么，如何确定开始收费的时机呢？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, there's a full pricing process here, so I'm happy to walk through it. The idea here is understanding who your customers are, why they pay you, what is it that they want or value, and how much are they willing to pay you. I'd encourage you to put together a pricing committee. This is not a single-threaded exercise that lives in one department or another. This very much is a cross-functional exercise. If you are a PLG company like companies I worked at, this was the product growth org that I ran. So the combination of PMs and data scientists, folks like that to iterate on pricing. If you are an enterprise SaaS business, of course, sales and finance and rev ops play a role. Think about who that committee should be at your company, and commit to being that cross-functional team that really owns and iterates on pricing over time. (20:31): Then, they are responsible for talking to customers. This is by far and away the most basic thing you can do to just increase those feedback loops and understand how much you can push the envelope on pricing. You do that with surveys, with interviews, there's some questions that we like to use around understanding the relative prioritization of features. Going back to that laundry list of features and matrices on a pricing page, it's very rare that people convert equally across all of those features. There's typically one or two that are the main points for conversion. So it's good for you to understand the relative rank there and how to reconcile some of your pricing and packaging accordingly. So, we would make a list of our features that we had and maybe new things we wanted to build and have people rank them as a must-have, nice to have, or not necessary that help us understand the relative prioritization. (21:23): You can also get at it with a hundred point question where you give users a hundred points and say, "Spend them across these different features." And the more points you give a feature, the more value you're assigning to it. This is to get to the demand or the features and functionality that you've created. It's step one. It's understanding what people will actually want and making sure that they're not just saying everything but the kitchen sink, but they're actually getting a good sense for what's most important to them. And then the other side is understanding their willingness to pay. I'd say the easiest on-ramps here for companies to start digging into that is to use Van Westendorp's method here. I don't know if you're familiar with that. You're nodding a little bit.
turns.zh:
是的，这里有一个完整的定价流程，我很乐意为您详细解析。关键在于了解客户是谁、他们为何付费、他们想要或重视什么，以及他们愿意为此支付多少费用。我建议您组建一个定价委员会。这不是单一部门的事情，而是跨职能的工作。对于像我曾就职的PLG公司，这类工作由产品增长团队负责。因此，需要产品经理、数据科学家等多方协作，不断优化定价策略。如果您是面向企业的SaaS公司，销售、财务和营收运营部门同样重要。思考一下贵公司应该组建怎样的委员会，并致力于打造这样一个跨职能团队，长期负责定价策略的制定与优化。
（20:31）：然后，他们需要与客户沟通。这是提升反馈循环、了解定价上限的最基本手段。您可以通过调查、访谈来收集数据，特别是关于功能相对优先级的反馈。回到定价页面上的功能列表，用户往往不会对所有功能都做出同等响应，通常有1-2个功能是转化主力。因此，了解这些功能的相对优先级，并据此调整定价和套餐组合至关重要。我们会列出现有功能及拟开发的新功能，让用户将分数分配到必需、可有可无或无关紧要的选项中，从而了解用户的相对优先级。
（21:23）：您还可以通过“100分问卷”来获取数据。给用户100分，让他们在不同功能间分配分数，得分越高的功能越受重视。这能让我们深入了解用户对所创建的功能和体验的需求。第一步是理解用户的实际需求，确保他们不只是面面俱到，而是能准确把握最重要的东西。另一方面，了解他们的支付意愿也很重要。我认为企业最容易入手的方法是应用范·韦斯滕多普（Van Westendorp）定价法。不知道您是否熟悉这个方法？您点头示意了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Comes up a bunch on this podcast.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。在这个播客里这个话题出现得可多了。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Oh, great. So I might be repeating myself here, but...
turns.zh: 哦，太好了。所以我可能在这里重复了一遍，但...

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, this is great. This is how we learn. We hear it again.
turns.zh: 不，这样很棒。这就是我们学习的方式。我们会再次听到这些观点。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: If you take the packages that users designated as nice to have and must have, you make that collection of features in the survey, then ask them, "What's such a cheap price that you start to question the quality of the product?" Ask them, "What's a good deal or sounds like the right price for this package?" Ask them, "What's expensive, but they would still pay?" So you're starting to get to that level of discomfort. And then ultimately, "What's prohibitively expensive? What would people just say, 'Okay, that's it.' You've crossed the line of how much I'm willing to pay here." And by plotting those four curves, you start to get a sense of how to inform your pricing. That's a great way to marry the questions around demand and then the questions around willingness to pay.
turns.zh: 如果你收集用户指定的“可有可无”和“必须拥有”的功能列表，然后在调查中询问他们：“什么样的价格低到让你开始怀疑产品的质量？”再问他们：“什么样的价格划算，或者听起来价格合适？”最后问他们：“什么样的价格太贵了，但他们还是愿意支付？”这样就能逐渐触及用户的接受底线了。最后，“什么样的价格高到让人直接放弃？”这就是用户愿意支付的最高价格界限。通过绘制这四条曲线，你就能了解如何制定定价策略了。这是一个将需求分析和支付意愿研究结合起来的绝佳方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I wish that survey name was simpler to say, because I can never remember exactly to pronounce it, but you got it. So Van Westendorp.
turns.zh: 太棒了。真希望那个调查名称能更简洁些，因为我总记不住准确发音，不过你已经理解了。所以，范·韦斯滕多普。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: You got it.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, say that you got a price, you launched with something. How do you think about and how do you suggest folks experiment with pricing changes? And then, what impact have you seen from making a pricing change, either in terms of revenue or growth? Because I know you work with a lot of startups on these sorts of things, so I'm curious. How big of an impact can you see from pricing changes?
turns.zh: 假设你确定了一个价格，推出了产品。那么你如何思考并建议人们尝试调整定价呢？调整定价后，无论是在收入还是增长方面，都产生了什么样的影响？因为我知道你为很多初创公司做过这方面的咨询，所以我很好奇。定价调整能带来多大的影响？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Oh, it can be huge. Our friends at OpenView do a really good job of pumping out content and doing these great SaaS benchmarking surveys. They did something recently that showed that roughly half of companies that instituted a pricing change saw at least a 25% increase in ARR. So that's a pretty massive step function improvement in your revenue from something that doesn't require massive technological overhaul. I find that most companies regret not doing it sooner. ProfitWell is another group that I have friends at and have a lot of respect for them and the content that they've put out. They did a survey once on I think it was over 500 SaaS companies, and they looked at for a 1% improvement on acquisition, retention, and monetization, how did it impact a company's bottom line? And they found that the impact with an improvement on monetization was 4X that of acquisition. (24:13): So, this idea of how can you efficiently improve your business monetization is really underappreciated as a growth lever. Definitely something people should be thinking about. That's part of my goal of doing this podcast, is making sure founders are compensated in a way that they deserve. So, let's hope everyone makes a little more money after today. And I've seen a lift upwards of 10X on revenue, but it's sometimes hard to parsh just the pricing change, because usually it can be coupled with big product changes, a rebrand, a lot of PR, the launch of a new plan, like a team or an enterprise plan. So, it's hard to sometimes understand just the pricing change in isolation, but it really can be pivotal.
turns.zh: 哦，影响可能非常大。我们在 OpenView 的朋友在内容创作和 SaaS 基准调查方面做得很出色。他们最近的一项研究显示，大约一半实施定价调整的公司，ARR 至少增长了 25%。这是一个不需要大规模技术改造就能显著提升收入的巨大跳跃。我发现大多数公司都后悔没有早点行动。ProfitWell 也是一个我很欣赏的团队，他们发布的内容也很棒。他们曾对 500 多家 SaaS 公司进行调查，研究获取客户、留存和变现这三个维度提升 1%对公司利润的影响。结果发现，提高变现能力对利润的提升效果是获取客户和留存的 4 倍。（24:13）所以，如何高效提升业务变现能力作为增长杠杆，被严重低估了。这绝对是人们应该深思的问题。我做这个播客的部分目标就是确保创始人能获得应有的报酬。所以，希望今天听完后，大家都能多赚点钱。我曾见过收入增长超过 10 倍的案例，但有时很难单独归因于定价调整，因为通常它会与重大产品变更、品牌重塑、大量公关活动、新计划的推出（如团队或企业计划）相结合。所以，有时很难孤立地理解定价调整的作用，但它确实至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And when you think through the pricing changes that you've seen, is the impact often from raising the price just broadly? Is it segmenting more intelligently? Is it changing freemium versus paid? Is there a bucket you think of, like "Here's generally where the biggest impact ends up being?"
turns.zh: 不错。那么，当你回顾所经历的定价调整时，其影响通常来自于全面提升价格吗？还是更明智地进行用户细分？又或者是从免费增值模式转向付费模式？你是否能想到某种模式，比如“这类调整通常会产生最大影响”？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, it comes from doing it holistically. I think it's very rarely as impactful if you just pick a new price or just launch a new plan. I really think of it as rebalancing pricing and packaging overall. So it's doing this whole exercise of understanding what people actually want, what their willingness to pay is, and mapping it to that user journey like we talked about from single-player mode to multi-player, that first other person you connect with and have a workflow with, spreading it to your whole teams and ultimately spreading it wall to wall across an organization. So it's a longitudinal view of the user lifecycle and thinking about your whole business model holistically.
turns.zh: 是的，这需要从整体角度入手。如果只是随意调整价格或推出新套餐，影响通常微乎其微。我认为关键在于全面重构定价和产品组合。比如，要深入了解用户真正需求、他们的支付意愿，并将这些信息与用户旅程相结合——从单人模式到多人协作，从与首位联系人的工作流，到团队层面，再到全组织范围内的推广。这需要以纵向视角审视用户生命周期，并全面审视整个商业模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you can talk about any of these, but is there a company or an example that comes to mind where you did a pricing change and just talking about what they changed just to make this even more concrete?
turns.zh: 我不知道你能否谈及具体案例，但有没有哪家公司或实例的定价调整能更直观地说明问题？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I have a specific story there with one of our companies, Envoy. This is a fun one. He was just getting started. This is Envoy, the visitor registration tool that I'm sure a lot of people have used, especially before COVID.
turns.zh: 我有个具体的案例，来自我们的公司Envoy。这是个很有趣的例子。Envoy是一款访客登记工具，我相信很多人都用过，尤其是新冠疫情之前。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Probably mostly in SF, so I imagine folks in other countries don't know about it. Maybe describe it.
turns.zh: 可能主要在旧金山，所以其他国家的人可能不了解它。能否简单介绍一下？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah. So, if you visit an office instead of just signing in to that piece of paper in the lobby with your name and your email address and what time you checked in, it is a digital iPad based way of checking in and sharing information with the person you're visiting. And so, in talking to Larry and getting a feel for his evolution around pricing, he tells a story that I love. He was meeting with a big hospitality company, and the conversation was going really well. This prospect was really leaning in and excited about using Envoy, and the conversation shifted to pricing. So in that moment, because Larry was feeling some good vibes, he decided to 10X the price that he was typically charging people. So, just in the moment he decided to just go for it. Go out on a limb, and ask for 10X the typical price. (27:13): And in that moment, the exec said, "Okay, sure. Sounds good." Not a minute of hesitation, not a second of hesitation. And what he learned in that moment was that, one, he was wildly underpriced. It was very clear that he hadn't even thought about what the ceiling was. But the truth was he probably could have pushed it even further, considering there was no hesitation. So, what I encourage users to do, especially in these enterprise conversations, is to continue to ask for more, to understand where the upper bound might be, and to understand that it's okay sometimes to lose some deals due to price. Something on the order of 20 to 30% is reasonable so that you can get a sense for where the limit might be. The vast majority of companies are definitely undercharging like we discussed. So, go out on a limb like Larry at Envoy, and you can see that sometimes you can...
turns.zh: 是的。Envoy最初是为办公室场景设计的，用户无需在大堂签到表格，只需在iPad上登记姓名、邮箱和签到时间，并与访问对象共享信息。Larry与我们分享的定价策略案例让我印象深刻。他曾与一家大型酒店集团会面，谈判进展顺利。这位客户对Envoy非常感兴趣，讨论重点转向了定价。由于当时气氛正佳，Larry决定将原定价提高十倍。结果对方毫不犹豫地答应了。（27:13）从那一刻起，客户说：“好的，没问题。听起来不错。”没有一丝犹豫。Larry从中领悟到，首先他的定价过低；客户显然没有考虑过上限价位。但实际上，考虑到对方毫不犹豫地接受涨价，涨价空间本可以更大。所以我鼓励用户，尤其是在与企业客户沟通时，要不断提升定价目标，了解潜在的上限价位，并接受因价格导致的部分交易流失。20%到30%的涨幅是合理的，这样能帮助你判断上限在哪里。绝大多数公司确实存在定价过低的问题。所以要像Envoy的Larry那样大胆尝试，你会发现有时候……

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: ... like Larry at Envoy and you can see that sometimes you can 2X, 4X, even 10X your price.
turns.zh: 比如Envoy公司的Larry所讲的案例，你可以看到有时候你能把价格翻两倍、四倍，甚至十倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome story and it touches on exactly what you said where people often underprice. I imagine it's strategically smarter not to go straight to 10X and maybe go two or three X until people start pushing back because you lose a lot of data there. But that's one way to just zoom to an answer.
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的故事，它正好印证了你所说的——人们常常低估自己的定价价值。我觉得从策略上讲，先不直接跳到十倍，而是先逐步提高两三倍，可能更明智，因为那样你会丢失大量数据。但这也是一种快速找到答案的方法。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, they're all feedback loops, so I think there's some incrementality to it. But you got to understand who these different segments are, and if you don't have enough data points, it's hard to really understand how to continue to optimize.
turns.zh: 是的，这些都是反馈循环，所以我认为其中存在递增效应。但你得理解不同客户群体的差异，如果数据点不足，就很难真正理解如何持续优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other tips that you want to leave listeners with around pricing or monetization, or even testing pricing? Anything there before we shift to our second topic?
turns.zh: 你还有什么关于定价或变现，甚至测试定价的建议想留给听众吗？在我们转到第二个话题之前，还有什么要补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yes. So we talked a bit about research methods and different surveys you can do to help inform your pricing. And with Enterprise, it's all about continuously asking for more. But if you're a PLG company and you have a public facing pricing page, I'd encourage you to experiment. This is something people shy away from, and frankly, there haven't historically been great tools for companies and infrastructure to be able to do this work. (29:08): So at Invoice2go, we invested very heavily in some internal pooling. We had a whole metering and human management and experimentation system in-house. It was a big growth engineering undertaking. And with that we tested different value metrics. We tested different quota limits, price points, promotions, you name it. We tracked the consumption of our pay as you go model and looped that back into the product so we can nudge users along the lifecycle to get them to convert, or upgrade or renew, once quota limits were reached. (29:38): So there's a lot there. I'm excited about this new wave of modern tools to actually help you do this and not sync a bunch of engineering time into building something in-house. So that's something we can talk about in a bit. But that investment was very worthwhile. We had huge revenue gains by being able to iterate in a way that was more streamlined. (29:57): There's some things to watch out for though. It's hard to test pricing. There's a lot of different variables to isolate. So you've got to make sure you're bringing a consistent test experience to the in product experience, your pricing page, maybe mobile app stores or lifecycle emails that you're sending. (30:14): One trick you can do is we would segment these tests by geo. So we would do some tests in Canada or Australia before rolling out in the US. That was a nice way to just put some constraints around our experimentation. (30:28): And the other thing you really have to think about is the long-term nature of pricing experimentation. So knowing if you succeeded and failed often requires understanding the implications on churn. Let's say part of your test is year one discount. You need to understand how users perform in year two and have a sense of the trade-offs around user growth, retention, ARPU. So all of these things are different levers that you want to optimize over time.
turns.zh:
是的。我们之前谈到了一些研究方法，以及可以进行的不同调查来辅助定价决策。对于企业客户来说，关键在于持续索要更多资源。但如果你是PLG公司，并且有面向公众的定价页面，我鼓励你进行实验。这是人们通常回避的事情，而且历史上一直没有优秀的工具能帮助企业和基础设施完成这项工作。
（29:08）：在Invoice2go，我们在内部投入了大量资源。我们内部建立了完整的计量和人工管理及实验系统。这是一项重大的增长工程任务。通过这种方式，我们测试了不同的价值指标、配额限制、价格点、促销活动等等。我们追踪了我们的按需付费模式的使用情况，并将其反馈到产品中，以便在用户达到配额限制后，引导他们完成整个生命周期——转化为付费用户、升级或续费。
（29:38）：这里有很多内容。我对现代工具的新浪潮感到兴奋，它们能真正帮助你实现这一目标，而不必投入大量工程时间来构建内部系统。这是我们稍后可以讨论的内容。但那次投资非常值得。通过更流畅的迭代方式，我们获得了巨大的收入增长。
（29:57）：不过需要注意一些问题。测试定价很难，需要隔离许多不同变量。因此，你必须确保在产品体验、定价页面、移动应用商店或发送的生命周期邮件中，提供一致的测试体验。
（30:14）：一个技巧是按地理区域划分测试。我们会在加拿大或澳大利亚进行测试，然后再在美国推出。这是给实验设置约束的好方法。
（30:28）：另外，你还必须考虑定价实验的长期性。要知道测试是否成功或失败，往往需要理解对客户流失的影响。假设你的测试部分是第一年的折扣，你需要了解用户在第二年的表现，并清楚用户增长、留存、每用户平均收入之间的权衡。所有这些都是你希望随着时间推移进行优化的不同杠杆。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, if you know that you have a bridge to move up market, then giving up the long tail of individual users can be very worthwhile. (32:50): So I think Figma is a great example of that. This was a company that took a while to monetize. And even having free usage at the individual level, that was the way to just drive insane community and love for this product. Designers around the world just fell for this product overnight. But this idea that once they were using it in a more corporate setting, once they were collaborating with more people across the business, they were tripping a wire to pay. And so what happened there was you had this massive top of funnel of individual users, but knowing that design is inherently collaborative, you're interfacing with engineers, you're interfacing with PMs, with marketers, with researchers, with execs, more than half of Figma users weren't even designers once it was embedded in the enterprise. And so this idea of these compounded growth loops that you got by interfacing with so many different parts of the company and making design truly collaborative and in the browser, they were able to just have this exponential curve on monetization once they shifted into more of a team or enterprise based package. (33:54): So that's a good example of saying, they were willing to trade off on monetizing the individual because they knew that it would be so sticky and would go so wall to wall within a company.
turns.zh: 是的，如果你清楚自己需要提升市场定位，那么放弃个人用户的长尾市场可能非常值得。（32:50）：我认为Figma就是一个很好的例子。这家公司花了很长时间才实现盈利。即使在个人层面提供免费使用，也是推动用户社区蓬勃发展、让用户爱上这款产品的有效策略。全球设计师一夜之间就被这款产品深深吸引。但当他们将其应用于企业环境、与更多团队成员协作时，用户愿意为此付费。于是出现了这样一种局面：虽然最初吸引了大量个人用户，但设计本质上是协作性的，用户需要与工程师、产品经理、市场营销人员、研究人员和高管合作。一旦Figma进入企业级应用阶段，超过半数的用户甚至都不是专业设计师。通过与公司各个部门深度融合，将设计真正打造成协作性工具，Figma得以实现用户增长的指数级增长，一旦转向团队或企业级付费模式，盈利曲线便急剧攀升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So your feeling is if it's a multiplayer PLG-ish product, you probably want to optimize for growth. Let it just take over and not go charge as much as you can immediately, versus say like a sales led B2B enterprise-y product, maybe they're focused on revenue immediately versus making it feel cheap. Is that right?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你的观点是，如果这是一款多人在线的PLG类产品，你可能更倾向于以增长为导向，先让产品迅速占领市场，而不是一开始就尽可能高价定价。相反，比如面向B2B企业的销售驱动型产品，可能更关注短期收益而非让用户觉得产品价格过高。对吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: And I think if you do have a few free users, crafting it as more of a sweetheart discount, like more of a year one discount, but getting paid over time. I mean, again, I am a big believer in having some early users being your design partners and really giving you that tight feedback loop to make sure you're building the right product. So it's not that you should really optimize for revenue on day one. I mean, it is a journey, but I just oftentimes see companies just take too long. Or in Evernote's case, I mean the free version was just too good. So that's just something to consider, where to put the paywall and be really, really strategic about that.
turns.zh: 我认为如果你有一些免费用户，可以把这当作一种优惠折扣，比如第一年的折扣，逐步实现收费。再说一次，我非常认同让早期用户成为你的设计伙伴，通过紧密的反馈循环确保产品方向正确。所以没必要在第一天就追求高收入。这确实是一个渐进的过程，但我经常看到很多公司拖延太久。拿Evernote来说，免费版做得太好了。所以在设置付费门槛时，要非常谨慎地考虑策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just don't optimize for guilt in your paid driver. (35:07): So you're talking about pricing testing and I was going to ask what tools you found that are useful for testing pricing. And that's probably a good segue to talking about the modern growth stack. Would that fit into this concept of modern growth stack, testing your pricing?
turns.zh: 别为了让用户感到内疚而优化付费模式。（35:07）：你提到了价格测试，我想问你用过哪些有效的测试工具。这或许是个过渡到现代增长栈的好机会。测试价格是否也属于现代增长栈的范畴？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it.
turns.zh: 是的，就这么办吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's do it. So just to set it up, there's this term modern data stack that I think it'd be useful for you to explain because not everyone is aware of that, and you've kind of been thinking more about this adjacent idea of a modern growth stack. So can you just talk about these two things, and then we'll lead to some questions there?
turns.zh: 好的，那我们开始吧。首先，我想跟大家解释一下“现代数据栈”这个术语，可能很多人对它不太熟悉。你最近一直在思考与之相似的“现代增长栈”概念，能否先讲讲这两个概念，再来回答大家的问题？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: So the modern data stack is basically a collection of cloud native tools to more easily move and manage data. It consists of a fully managed ELT, data pipeline, a destination for that data. So a cloud-based data warehouse, like a Snowflake or Redshift, data transformation tool like DBT, and then finally a platform for visualization on top, so people can access the data. The play on modern data stack was very intentional. I think of the modern growth stack, or my core thesis area right now at Menlo, as the evolution of what you do with the data. So these are the workflows that the data enables to drive the business forward for product growth and revenue teams like I used to run. It's the modern replacement for infrastructure that teams like mine built or bought. When you're responsible for driving things like activation or monetization or retention, there tends to be a lot of these internal tools that are built because you're really powering cross-functional teams to do this work. It's not mapped easily into legacy departments.
turns.zh: 现代数据栈本质上是集合了一系列云原生工具，用于更便捷地迁移和管理数据。它由以下几个部分组成：完全托管的ELT（提取、加载、转换）和数据管道、数据目标（如Snowflake或Redshift等云数据仓库）、数据转换工具（如DBT），以及最终的可视化平台，方便用户访问数据。之所以称之为“现代数据栈”，是有深意的。在我看来，现代增长栈，或者说我目前在Menlo公司关注的核心领域，是数据应用场景的进化。它所支持的工作流，推动着像我曾负责的产品增长和营收团队这样的业务前进。这是替代传统基础设施的现代方案，而传统基础设施往往是我们团队自建或采购的。当你需要推动用户激活、变现或留存等业务时，往往会开发大量内部工具，因为你需要赋能跨职能团队完成这些工作。这些工具很难与传统部门的职能对接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And the general idea here is, there's so many more tools now to help you grow with the data stack. There's just all these tools now that make it so much easier to collect data, use data, make decisions off data, and you're finding the same things happening with growth. What are some of the tools that you found to be super helpful? I know you're an investor in some, you're not a investor in others. It'd be good to just talk about, here's just like a bunch of cool tools and how do they fit together as much as possible to help you grow your startup.
turns.zh: 太棒了。总的来说，这里有更多工具可以帮助你借助数据堆栈实现业务增长。现在有各种各样的工具，让收集数据、利用数据、基于数据做决策变得容易得多，你会发现增长策略中也有类似的思路。你们发现哪些工具特别有用？我知道有些工具你投资了，有些则没有。能不能跟我们分享一下，哪些酷炫的工具能最大程度地协同合作，助力创业公司发展？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: And I want to reinforce some different themes before I get into some layers of the stack because I think it's important to frame the benefits of the modern growth stack. So one is data, two is workflow, and three is impact. (37:18): So starting with data, the modern growth stack companies really are powered by these smart integrations and the automation that you get as a result. So with this proliferation of SaaS, it's created this need for more data access and interoperability. We've all felt that pain of siloed data. Modern growth stack companies leverage reverse ETL companies, like Hightouch or Census, to break down these silos and help companies, or employees across the company, access data and be more productive. So that's a big data theme with modern growth stack companies. (37:49): The other theme that they unlock is around workflow. Here, it's really the enablement of people and process. So rather than employees sitting in their departmental silos, modern growth stack companies build bridges between them. So by unlocking data access, the business side can often self-serve and be more self-sufficient without relying on an engineer or a data scientist to run queries or stitch together data sets for them. (38:16): The other thing here is lots of growth work is inherently cross functional. So the efforts to drive growth requires new tools and collaborative workflows like we're discussing. Without purpose-built software, many teams like mine felt no choice but to build in-house. So we spent sacred hours building and maintaining tooling for experimentation, personalization, billing, monetization. These were resources that could have been reallocated to building proprietary features for the business had we been able to buy something purpose-built. (38:50): And finally, these products really drive impact. So the idea here is driving hard ROI in the form of cost reduction. So automation means time savings, and oftentimes, that can be mapped directly to cost reduction for a company. But they also help product and growth and go to market teams better engage and monetize customers. So they're driving hard ROI in the form of revenue impact too. I'm really compelled by companies that can drive hard ROI both across cost saving and revenue generation. And I think that ROI story is even more compelling now in a softer macroeconomic climate. You just have to be able to continue to retain sales and pricing power, and I think that's derived from a strong ROI story like I described. (39:35): So those are general themes and consistencies across the companies that I get particularly excited about. So happy to talk about a few layers in the stack, and I think you might be familiar with a few of these as well, especially based on your growth background at Airbnb and tools that you probably build yourself.
turns.zh:
在深入探讨数据堆栈的各个层级之前，我想先强调几个核心主题，因为我认为理解现代增长堆栈的优势至关重要。首先是数据，其次是工作流程，最后是影响力。（37:18）：先从数据说起，现代增长堆栈公司真正依赖于智能集成和由此带来的自动化。随着SaaS的普及，数据访问和互操作性的需求也随之产生。我们都深有体会数据孤岛带来的困扰。现代增长堆栈公司借助逆向ETL工具（如Hightouch或Census）打破数据孤岛，让企业员工更高效地获取数据。数据访问是现代增长堆栈公司的核心主题。

（37:49）：另一个突破点是工作流程的优化。这里关键在于赋能人员和流程。传统上，员工被困在部门孤岛中，而现代增长堆栈公司通过搭建桥梁打破这些隔阂。通过开放数据访问，业务部门能够自主服务，无需依赖工程师或数据科学家来运行查询或整合数据集。

（38:16）：许多增长工作本质上是跨职能的。推动增长需要新的工具和协作工作流，比如我们正在讨论的这些。没有专门开发的软件，像我这样的团队只能自建工具。例如，我们耗费大量精力构建和维护实验、个性化、计费和变现的工具。如果当时能购买现成的工具，这些资源本可以重新分配到开发专有功能上。

（38:50）：最后，这些产品能带来显著的业务影响。核心在于以成本降低的形式推动高ROI。自动化节省时间，这往往能直接转化为公司的成本削减。同时，它们还能帮助产品和增长团队更好地吸引和变现客户。因此，它们也以收入增长的形式推动高ROI。我对那些能在成本节省和收入增长两方面都实现高ROI的公司深感敬佩。在当前宏观经济环境疲软的情况下，这样的ROI故事显得更加引人注目。你必须能够持续保持销售和定价能力，而这正源于我所描述的强劲ROI故事。

（39:35）：以上就是我特别感兴趣的公司的共性主题。很乐意和大家探讨堆栈的各个层级，我相信你们也对其中一些有所了解，特别是基于你在Airbnb的增长经验和可能自主开发的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. That's what I was going to say, that so many of these things are just coming out of startups that have built these in-house. And then they're just like, "Hey, I could start a company doing this and provide it to all these other companies." And so I just love that there's all these tools coming out that just make it easier to build startups and grow startups, and do less work, and have less people. Just reminds me of the number one app in the App Store at this point. I don't know if it still is Gas, which is just like four people, and it's higher than TikTok and YouTube, and all the things, and Facebook, and it's four people. And so it just shows you the power of what tools can do for you to build new startups and disrupt people, and companies that have been around for a long time.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。我正想说呢，许多这类产品都是由内部开发的初创公司推出的。然后他们就会说：“嘿，我可以创办一家公司来提供这项服务，再把它卖给其他公司。”所以我特别欣喜于市面上涌现出这些工具，它们能让初创公司更轻松地创立和发展业务，减少工作量，降低人力成本。这让我想起了应用商店里目前排名第一的应用。我不知道它是否还叫Gas，但那家公司只有四个人。它的排名却高于TikTok、YouTube、Facebook等巨头。这充分说明了工具能为初创公司赋能，颠覆传统企业，创造惊人价值。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: And you have to help companies do more with less now. There's a lot of frozen budgets and that's a good way to break through. So I love that these companies can do that for the buyer. (40:44): So one that's come up a bit and gotten a lot of airtime recently is product-led sales. This idea of companies that serve PLG businesses and harness the power of all that product usage data to inform the customer facing team around which accounts are most upgradable. It's really free money when you shine a light on an account that nobody was paying attention to and some inside sales team can drive a large account expansion. So I don't know what better ROI you should get than that. (41:14): And there's a bunch of companies that are doing this. Endgame happens to be one that I work with. They have customers like Figma, Loom, Calendly. There's other players too. I think Pocus has done a phenomenal job of building content and community to help inform the market around the power of product led sales. So there's just a lot of goodness about all the players in this space really waking everyone up to this opportunity of layering on sales to a product led motion and how to maximize revenue along the way.
turns.zh: 如今，企业必须用更少的资源做更多的事。预算被冻结，而这正是突破困境的良机。所以我很欣赏这些公司能为客户提供增值服务（40:44）：最近备受关注且广受瞩目的是产品主导型销售模式。这种模式下，服务PLG企业的公司能充分利用产品使用数据，帮助销售团队锁定最具升级潜力的客户。当你聚焦那些被忽视的客户时，就能轻松挖掘潜在价值，内部销售团队就能推动大客户拓展。这样的投资回报率简直无与伦比。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm an investor in both of those actually, and I'm going to, just in the show notes, note the one I'm an investor in because I'm investor in a lot of these companies, it turns out. And we've invested in a few, so I'm just going to keep it simple and I'll write in the show notes. Here's ones I'm an investor, just to avoid.
turns.zh: 这个领域有很多优秀的公司。Endgame恰好是我合作的客户之一，他们的客户包括Figma、Loom、Calendly等，还有其他参与者。Pocus在内容建设和社区运营方面做得非常出色，帮助市场认识到产品主导型销售的强大力量，以及如何通过将销售与产品结合来最大化收益。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I love that. Double- dipping means you're a believer in the category as well.
turns.zh: 实际上，我在这两家公司都是投资者。为了避免混淆，我会在节目笔记中注明我投资的公司，因为我投资了不少这类公司。我们已经投了几个项目，所以我会保持简洁，直接写在节目笔记里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种双重获益的方式，这说明你也看好这个领域。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: ... tipping means you're a believer in the category as well.
turns.zh: ……投资意味着你也看好这个领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am. I love it. There's so much school stuff happening there and I'm really excited. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我很喜欢。这里有很多教育类产品正在兴起，我非常兴奋。是啊。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yep. Cool. I think another layer in the stack is experimentation. So this is really critical infrastructure, in my opinion, for these cross-functional product data growth teams to A/B test hypotheses and understand their impact on the business. How do you know if you make a change in the product or your pricing, whether you succeeded or failed without having infrastructure like this along the way? Category creators like Optimizely really paved the way. I was an early buyer of Optimizely and they targeted marketing personas, and it was just game changing to be able to start to A/B test things and bring hypotheses to life. (42:44): I'm also biased as an investor, but some of the modern tools here, like Eppo, which offers experimentation for the modern data stack. So unlike Optimizely, which focused on more kind of click through metrics, Eppo ties directly to the metrics in your data warehouse. So tying an experiment result to things like subscriptions or revenue or margins, really like board level metrics that you're trying to move. They make that full trip really convenient and understand the impact on those business KPIs directly. So it's a lot of automation around the experimentation, results. And analysis they used to live off to the side in Excel or Jupyter Notebooks now is automated away with Eppo. I think you're familiar with that one.
turns.zh: 是的。太棒了。我认为，在我看来，另一个关键的数据基础设施是实验。这样一来，跨职能的产品数据增长团队就能对假设进行A/B测试，并了解其对业务的影响。如果没有这样的基础设施，当你对产品或定价进行改动时，如何判断是成功还是失败呢？像Optimizely这样的公司确实开辟了先路。作为Optimizely的早期用户，我发现他们针对营销人员的定位功能，真正改变了游戏规则，让我们能够开始进行A/B测试，将假设变为现实。（42:44）：作为投资者，我也难免有偏见，但现在有一些现代工具，比如Eppo，为现代数据栈提供了实验功能。与Optimizely主要关注点击率等指标不同，Eppo直接与数据仓库中的指标相连。因此，将实验结果与订阅量、收入或利润等业务关键指标关联起来，真正触及你试图推动的董事会级别指标。这样一来，实验、结果和分析就完全自动化了，而这些原本需要在Excel或Jupyter Notebook中手动处理的工作，现在通过Eppo得以自动化处理。我相信你对这个工具很熟悉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we definitely didn't plan this, but Eppo's both a happy sponsor of this podcast. I'm also an investor in Eppo. Go Eppo, but this was not planned.
turns.zh: 是的，我们确实没有计划这样做，但Eppo是本播客的赞助商。我也是Eppo的投资者。Eppo加油，不过这不是刻意安排的。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Well, this is Airbnb roots. [inaudible 00:43:41].
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是Airbnb的根源。[00:43:41的音频模糊]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it. It is. Yeah. It's my colleague.

turns.en: [inaudible 00:43:42] was an early data scientist at Airbnb.
turns.zh: [00:43:42的音频模糊]曾是Airbnb的早期数据科学家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly, I worked with him at Airbnb and he was amazing and I had to invest in anything that he built. He built an awesome thing.
turns.zh: 没错，我在Airbnb和他共事过，他非常出色，我必须投资他开发的任何产品。他创造了一个很棒的东西。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yeah, but exactly like you describe, I love these founders that have steep authenticity around the problem because they built it internally and now they're commercializing it for the masses. And so the story of chain Eppo is a good one on that dimension. And there's other players too. I'm also a big fan of Amplitude and a buyer of that tool as well, and I love a lot of the team there. So if you do not have a data team or a data warehouse and you still want to leverage being able to do behavioral kind of ad hoc analysis or experimentation, that's a great tool for you as well. So a lot of different ways to solve this problem in the market.
turns.zh: 是的，但正如你所描述的，我喜欢这些创始人，他们对问题有深刻的理解，因为他们内部开发了产品，现在将其商业化供大众使用。因此，Eppo的故事在这方面很棒。还有其他参与者。我也是Amplitude的忠实粉丝，也是该工具的买家，我喜欢那里的很多团队。所以，如果你没有数据团队或数据仓库，但仍然想利用行为类型的临时分析或实验能力，这对你们来说也是一个很棒的工具。市场上有许多不同的解决问题的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, a happy sponsor, go Amplitude.
turns.zh: 同样，作为赞助商，很高兴Amplitude能参与其中。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. This is great. Hitting on all my favorites. Okay, let's keep going. What else have we got?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样。这太棒了。满足了我所有喜好的需求。好的，我们继续吧。还有什么内容呢？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Well, I talked a lot about billing and monetization, so I'd have to talk about that one. I think platforms for managing, billing and iterating on your pricing and packaging, this is just such a big need. I think these will transform business models. For SaaS in particular, most companies have been seat-based like we described, so the historical incumbents like a [inaudible 00:44:54] really serve that model. But in this shift to more usage based, there's new entrants that are servicing companies in that dimension. And there's also lots of sort of clunky workflows when you think of bridging from engineering to product and growth to finance or RevOps. (45:11): So there's a lot of just streamlined workflow that these new tools can offer. Some early breakout players in the world of usage-based billing are Metronome and Orb. There's also more room to handle the full monetization infra-layer. So for example, I like how Orb marries the billing component with the data infrastructure to actually inform what your pricing and packaging iteration should be and help you forecast and optimize revenue. So there's other players that are doing different components from this journey of the metering piece all the way through to the experimentation piece, and it's been really, really fun to get to know players in that space. And I wish I could have been a buyer of them many moons ago.
turns.zh: 嗯，我之前讲了很多关于计费和变现的部分，所以我得再聊聊这个话题。我认为用于管理、计费以及迭代定价和打包策略的平台，目前存在着巨大的市场需求。这些平台将彻底改变商业模式。特别是对于SaaS领域，大多数公司一直采用我们之前提到的座位授权模式，因此像[音频模糊00:44:54]这样的传统巨头仍在主导这一模式。但在向基于使用量计费转型的过程中，出现了新的市场参与者，专门为企业提供相关解决方案。此外，当你考虑从工程团队到产品团队，再到财务或收入运营团队的衔接时，会发现整个流程存在诸多低效环节。（45:11）：因此，新工具能够显著优化这些流程。基于使用量计费领域的早期领军企业有Metronome和Orb。同时，整个变现基础设施层也存在着巨大的优化空间。比如，我很欣赏Orb将计费组件与数据基础设施相结合，帮助企业优化定价和打包策略，并实现收入预测和优化。还有其他公司在从计量模块到实验测试的整个变现路径中提供不同组件，深入了解这些公司的发展历程真是非常有趣。真希望自己多年前就能成为他们的投资者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not an investor in these yet. And so that's cool. Quick tangent, do you have a strong opinion on pricing models, usage based versus seed based versus something else? What's your guidance to founders? Is this the way to go, usually one of them, or is it super dependent? What do you recommend?
turns.zh: 目前我还没有投资这些公司，不过这也很棒。顺便问一下，你对计费模式有何看法？基于使用量计费、基于座位授权还是其他模式？对创始人有什么建议？通常是选择其中一种模式，还是高度依赖具体情况？你会如何推荐？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Yes, this is a similar answer I had before. I don't think that they're mutually exclusive. And so if you look at all the companies that in different pricing models in SaaS, a small sliver less than 10%, around roughly 5% have just pure natural escalator kind of usage-based model. The vast majority have a hybrid approach. And so what I mean by that is they're typically some good, better, best subscription model where there's some consumption component across each tier, like some quota limit for your given value metric. So in Slack there might have been number of messages sent or Dropbox number of terabytes of storage. Invoice2go might be number of invoices. There's some dimension that's been sort of packaged in with a given pricing plan, and once you reach that limit, it is a trigger to get you to upgrade to the next plan over, or sometimes there's overages that you can pay for. (47:02): So I don't believe that you should just be seat-based or just be usage-based. I think one challenge with purely usage-based models is that's not always how CFOs want to buy. I think buyers sometimes want predictability. They want to be able to budget for your tool, and I've lived that. I remember using tools like Mixpanel and Segment and even Jira to an extent where I was paying a cheap amount to get going, and all of a sudden I realized we had grown quickly and I looked at all of our SaaS spend and I was blown away by how much more we were paying. So it's the other side of this... I'm advocating for people getting paid and compensated for the value that they're delivering, but there can be a breaking point. And so how do you think about packaging a fixed and variable component so that people can more predictably buy your software?
turns.zh: 是的，我之前也说过类似观点。两种模式并非相互排斥。以SaaS领域为例，采用不同定价模式的公司中，仅有不到10%（约5%）采用纯粹的基于使用量的计费模式。绝大多数公司采用混合策略。具体来说，他们通常会构建“好、更好、最好”的订阅模式，每个层级都包含一定的消费组件，比如针对特定价值指标的配额限制。例如，Slack可能设定消息发送数量上限，Dropbox设定存储容量限制，Invoice2go设定发票数量限制等。每个定价计划都包含某种预设维度，一旦达到上限，用户就会被触发升级到下一个计划，有时还可支付超额费用。（47:02）：我认为不应局限于座位授权或单纯的基于使用量计费模式。纯粹基于使用量的模式面临的挑战在于，CFO通常不愿采用这种计费方式。他们希望预见性更强，能为工具进行预算规划。我深有体会。记得我曾使用Mixpanel、Segment甚至Jira等工具时，最初花费不多，后来发现业务增长迅速，查看SaaS支出时惊讶于费用激增。这正说明了另一面……我主张让开发者因其创造的价值获得合理报酬，但必须设定一个合理的平衡点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other layers of the stack that you want to touch on slash which would you be most excited about in the future? Do you think people should be paying more attention to that maybe they're not paying attention to?
turns.zh: 您还想谈谈堆栈中的其他任何层面，或者未来最令您兴奋的领域吗？您认为人们是否应该更加关注这些领域？或许他们目前关注得还不够？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I mean, I wouldn't be doing my job as a VC if I didn't mention Generative AI right now. It's really having a moment. So there's a bunch of breakout applications there that sit within this theme of the modern growth stack. When you think of using AI to create images or text or code or audio or video, these capabilities change the way teams work. So writing a blog or writing copy for an ad, SDR is doing their work and can outbound sales efforts. There's just a lot of these touchpoints where it's humans kind of tinkering and iterating and laboring over every word. And if the machine, if AI can tell you what's going to be a more performant version of something, that's a very, very hard ROI exercise there. You save time and hopefully you've improved your performance across the various marketing or sales campaign.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，如果我现在不提生成式人工智能，那我就没尽到风投的职责了。它现在确实风头正劲。在现代增长堆栈的主题下，涌现出一批突破性应用。当你想到用人工智能来创作图像、文本、代码、音频或视频时，这些能力正在改变团队的工作方式。比如写博客、为广告撰写文案，销售开发人员（SDR）开展外呼销售工作。有很多这样的接触点，人们通常需要反复修改每个字词。而如果机器、人工智能能告诉你什么样的版本更高效，那这就是一个非常非常高的投资回报率案例。你节省了时间，有望提升各种营销或销售活动的效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where do you think AI will be the most help on growth in terms of growth? Do you have an idea there?
turns.zh: 您认为在增长方面，AI将在哪些方面提供最大帮助？您对此有什么想法吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I think what I described around marketing and sales, just because they really touch the dollars. It can be this ROI story around saving time, but also driving revenue. There'll be plenty of really effective examples within things like customer support. I mean the cost savings potential. There's going to be massive. We'll see what happens in engineering, which generating code. I think there's a lot of areas where it is going to touch the enterprise, but from a modern growth stack standpoint, I think something that's really revenue generating and can point to attributable ROI on that dimension is going to be pretty relevant to where I'm spending time right now.
turns.zh: 我认为我刚才描述的市场营销和销售领域，是因为它们确实关乎实际收益。它可以讲述一个关于节省时间、同时推动收入增长的投资回报率故事。在客户支持等领域，也会有很多高效的案例。我是说节省成本的潜力将是巨大的。我们会看看工程领域会如何发展，比如生成代码。我认为有很多领域会触及企业，但从现代增长堆栈的角度来看，我认为真正能带来收入并能在该维度上指出可归因的投资回报率的东西，将与我目前投入精力的方向高度相关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited. Any last thoughts before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我很兴奋。在我们进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节之前，您还有什么最后的想法吗？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I'm happy to hand it over to the lightning round here.
turns.zh: 我很乐意将话题交给闪电问答环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, we've reached the very exciting lightning round. I'm only going to have four questions for you. I'm going to ask them pretty quick. We'll go through them fast, whatever comes to mind. No pressure. Question one, what are a couple books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，我们来到了令人兴奋的闪电问答环节。我只会向您提出四个问题。我会问得很快。我们会快速浏览，想到什么就说什么。别有压力。第一个问题，您向其他人推荐最多的几本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: My buddy Madhavan from Simon Kucher's wrote a book called Monetizing Innovation. This is a great read. He and others there have done pricing engagements with hundreds of tech companies, so there's a lot of stories and practical tips there. I often gift that one to founders, so I can't do this whole talk without giving a nod to my friend, Madhavan, and his bible.
turns.zh: 我来自西蒙·库彻的伙伴Madhavan写了一本叫《将创新变现》的书。这是一本很棒的读物。他和那里的其他人为数百家科技公司做过定价咨询，所以书中有很多故事和实用技巧。我经常把这本书送给创始人，所以在整个演讲中，我不能不向我的朋友Madhavan和他的这本宝典致敬。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I just recorded an episode with Madhavan, and so that's a great pick. Question number two, favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我刚和Madhavan录制了一期节目，所以这是个很棒的选择。第二个问题，最近您最喜欢、最享受的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I have little kids, so I don't know if this is going to be as interesting for folks, but we like Story Bots on Netflix. They're these little cartoon characters that answer kids questions. So people sort of call in and ask questions and they do a whole episode on why is the sky blue? How do airplanes fly? How do I see? And I inevitably learned something from watching those. So those are very kind of playful and educational shows. I critically need a new-
turns.zh: 我有孩子，所以不知道这对大家是否有趣，但我们很喜欢网飞上的《故事机器人》。这部动画片里的小卡通角色会回答孩子们的问题。比如有人打电话提问，他们就会做一整集节目，讲天空为什么是蓝的？飞机怎么飞的？我怎么能看见？我每次看都能学到东西。这类节目既有趣又有教育意义。我现在急需一部新剧——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, those are... I don't know the answer to any of those questions. I need to watch this. Okay, so question three. I'm looking at my notes and I've never asked this question before, so I don't know where this came from, but I love it. Who's been the biggest inspiration to you in your life?
turns.zh: 不，那些问题……我一个都答不上来。我得去看看。好的，第三个问题。我看笔记，之前从没问过这个问题，真不知道从哪儿冒出来的，但我很喜欢。谁是你人生中最大的灵感来源？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I mean, this one's pretty easy. For me, it's my parents. They're from South America originally and lived on three different continents before immigrating to the US for graduate school. It's a pretty cliché American dream, but they came here with nothing. Just this idea of building a family and taking advantage of the educational and professional opportunities in America. They progressed through school and building their career in three different languages with no financial support, no entrenched kind of resources or networks to lean on, and I just can't imagine doing that. Just the stress or cognitive load of kind of restarting your life in whole new geographies and cultures and languages and just betting on yourself and figuring it all out along the way. So my drive has always been rooted in their story and I'm forever indebted to them.
turns.zh: 这个问题挺简单的。对我来说，是我的父母。他们最初来自南美洲，在移民美国读研前曾在三个不同大洲生活过。这是典型的美国梦，但他们来时一无所有。只带着建立家庭、抓住美国教育和职业机会的想法。他们用三种语言在没有经济支持、缺乏资源和人脉的情况下完成学业和事业发展。我无法想象那种在全新地域、文化和语言中重建生活的压力，全凭自己摸索前行。所以我的动力始终源于他们的故事，我永远感激他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I need to ask this question more often. That was an amazing answer on the spot. Naomi, we have reached the end of our chat. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to learn more, maybe pitch you startup ideas, contact you if they want to ask you questions, and then finally, how can folks be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我得多问这种即兴回答的问题。娜奥米，我们的聊天结束了。最后两个问题。如果大家想了解更多信息、给创业想法、联系我提问，可以在哪儿找到我？

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: I'm a partner at Menlo Ventures, so you can find more about me in the firm at menlovc.com or else on LinkedIn or Twitter. My DMs are open.
turns.zh: 我是门洛风投的合伙人，可以在menlovc.com上了解更多信息，或者在领英和推特上找到我。私信随时开放。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Naomi, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。娜奥米，非常感谢你今天的参与。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: My pleasure. I look forward to talking to more folks who are building things across workflow automation, data AI, and the modern growth stack. So thank you. It's always a pleasure.
turns.zh: 不客气。我期待与更多在工作流自动化、数据人工智能和现代增长堆栈领域打造产品的伙伴交流。谢谢。总是很愉快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, DMs are coming in as we speak.
turns.zh: 好的，私信正在陆续到来。

turns.speaker: Naomi Ionita
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢，伦尼。
